newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Beijing speaks out as U.S. snubs China over HK.
newsitem.headline: Beijing speaks out as U.S. snubs China over HK.

text.p: The United States snubbed China on Tuesday by announcing that Secretary of State Madeleine Albright would boycott the investiture of Hong Kong's unelected legislature at the grand handover gala.
China fired back a propaganda volley, accusing certain people in the United States of harbouring "evil intentions" towards Hong Kong ahead of its return to Chinese rule.

In Hong Kong itself, the Democratic Party seized the moment to launch a last minute constititional challenge to the provisional legislature at the centre of the controversy, filing a writ in the High Court.
Britain and its Western allies have attacked the new assembly, questioning its legitimacy and the need for it to replace the democratically elected Legislative Council.

China had planned to swear in future leader Tung Chee-hwa, the future judiciary and the provisional chamber on July 1, shortly after a solemn midnight flag ceremony marking the end of 156 years of British rule and reunion with China.
U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Albright, a guest of honour at the handover ceremony, would not go to the swearing-in.
"I can tell you if she were invited, she would not attend that ceremony...because it wouldn't be appropriate," Burns said.
Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten hinted other Western leaders might behave the same way, but he left the world guessing about the intentions of new British Prime Minister Tony Blair.

"We know that the United States feels strongly about the provisional legislature and I guess that some other political leaders who believe in democracy and democratic institutions will have the same sort of concerns," Patten told reporters.
Speculation is rife that Blair might shun the handover ceremony if China attempts to inaugurate the legislature in the eyes of foreign VIPs, humiliating the outgoing British.
In Beijing, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Cui Tiankai said attendance would be optional at the flag ceremony and also the later swearing-in of new the Hong Kong administration,.
Beijing has yet to announce whether President Jiang Zemin would be present at the handover along with Premier Li Peng, although a Hong Kong newspaper said Jiang did plan to attend.
That would make him the first Chinese leader to set foot in Hong Kong since Britain seized it at gunpoint as spoils of victory in the 19th century Opium Wars.

China's defence establishment said that hostile U.S. forces were determined to interfere in Hong Kong ahead of the handover. Some people in the United States harboured "evil intentions" for the territory, the official China Defence newspaper said.

"Out of a need to maintain its global strategic position, the United States is strengthening its intelligence work in Hong Kong, supporting Hong Kong's Democratic Party and fostering political forces," its said.
"Before and after Hong Kong's return, some U.S. politicians and intermediaries will certainly stir up trouble over the Hong Kong issue."

With time running out -- there are only 21 days to go -- the Democratic Party finally filed a threatened writ accusing the provisional legislature of usurping the existing council's law-making powers.
Legal experts said the move had little chance of success but would cause acute embarrassment and may temporarily block the chamber's activities.

The 60-strong provisional assembly, which has met so far in China because of the doubts about its legality, was selected by a China-controlled panel in late 1996 to replace the existing chamber returned by about one million voters in a 1995 poll.
The Democrats, with 17 seats in the doomed chamber making it the largest party, boycotted the selection process for the shadow chamber, which it denounced as a travesty of democracy.

They face a year in the wilderness when the existing chamber is dissolved, wiping out at a stroke the mild democratic reforms instigated by the Patten that rid the chamber of appointed members and broadened the electorate.

Future leader Tung, a billionaire tycoon chosen to run Hong Kong by the same China-controlled electoral college that chose the shadow legislature, urged the Democratic Party to drop the legal action, but party leader Martin Lee vowed no surrender.
"This writ will not be cancelled... We told him we would definitely go ahead," Lee told reporters after meeting Tung.
Tung argued that the handover would be a joyous occasion and invited the Democrats to join him in "building a solid foundation for Hong Kong's future", a Tung spokesman said.
Earlier, Tung told Britain's Independent Television News that he was a principled individual and was ready to resign if the job clashed with his principles.
Tung's comment came just a week after his future number-two, Chief Secretary Anson Chan, made a similar statement, arousing speculation about tension between the two leaders.
"I would resign on matters of principle," Tung said. "We would all do it because it is important. As a person we all have our principles. We all have our vision. We all have our beliefs."
